Before the first dawn, the world was a dark bowl of water, and all creatures drifted without names. Above them slept Auru, the Sky-Turtle, whose shell was covered in tiny unlit stars. One night, a small silver fish grew tired of bumping into shadows. She leapt from the water and struck Auru’s shell with her tail.

“Wake,” she cried. “We cannot find one another.”

Auru opened one ancient eye. Seeing the lonely world below, he shook himself. One star fell from his shell and sank into the water. Where it touched, it became a glowing pearl, and around the pearl rose the first island.

The creatures climbed onto land, blinking in wonder. But the island was cold. So the silver fish leapt again and again, knocking loose more stars. Some became fireflies, some became flowers, and one great star became the sun.

Auru thanked the fish and gave her a name: Luma, Bringer of Light. Yet Luma missed the deep water. She dove back into the sea, carrying one spark beneath her scales.

That is why, even now, when moonlight touches waves, the ocean glimmers with silver memories of the fish who woke the sky.

Before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of dark water, and all creatures slept beneath its surface, dreaming of land. Only Mura, the little firebird, was awake. She had one glowing feather, no larger than a leaf, and she kept it hidden under her wing.

One night, the deep water whispered, “Nothing can grow while I cover everything.” Mura felt pity for the unborn forests and the mountains waiting without names. She flew upward until her wings ached and dropped her feather into the sky.

The feather burst into the sun.

Light poured over the waters, and the creatures opened their eyes. Turtles rose and became islands. Sleeping serpents stretched into rivers. The oldest whale lifted his back, and upon it appeared the first hill.

But Mura had given away her warmth. She fell, cold and gray, toward the new earth. The trees caught her gently and asked the sun to remember her. So each evening, when the sun sinks low, it paints the clouds red and gold in the shape of wings.

That is why birds sing at dawn: they are thanking Mura, who traded her fire so the world could wake.

Myth: Before the first morning, the world was a silent lake beneath a lid of stone, and every creature floated in dreams without shape or name. Only Nira, a moth with a lantern-heart, could see through the dark. Her glow was small, but it trembled with longing.

Below, seeds slept inside the water, unable to remember how to become trees. Above, mountains waited in the stone lid, folded like birds that had forgotten their wings. Nira heard them sigh.

“I am little,” she said, “but little light can begin a road.”

She flew upward until her soft wings tore against the stone. At last her lantern-heart brushed the roof of the world. A crack opened, and through it poured the first golden flame. The stone lid broke apart and rose into the sky as clouds. The sleeping mountains unfolded from the water, and the seeds climbed their slopes, becoming forests.

Nira fell, her lantern dimmed to ash. The new trees caught her and hid her gently among their leaves. To honor her, they asked the sky to scatter her sparks.

That is why moths circle lamps at night: they are seeking Nira’s lost heart, the first small light that opened the world.

That is why the sea shines at night, and why every island remembers the little fish who borrowed light from heaven.

In the highest darkness drifted Oru, the ancient turtle, carrying unawakened stars upon his back. In the lowest water swam Seli, a tiny fish with a bright blue heart.

That is why waves glitter beneath the moon, and why every dawn remembers the little fish who taught the dark to open.

Myth: Before the first sunrise, the world was a black ocean sealed beneath a roof of sleeping stone. Nothing had edges. Fish dreamed they were birds, seeds dreamed they were stars, and mountains dreamed in silence under the waves.

Only Vela, a tiny beetle with a coal of blue fire in her chest, was awake. She crawled across the water as if it were glass, listening to the unborn forests murmur below.

“We cannot grow,” they whispered. “We do not know which way is up.”

Vela looked at the stone roof and answered, “Then I will make an upward.”

She climbed a thread of mist until she reached the ceiling of the world. With her small horn she tapped once, twice, three times. The stone cracked. Her blue coal flared, and the crack widened into dawn.

Light spilled through. The ocean drew back in wonder, revealing valleys, hills, and sleeping roots. The mountains lifted their heads. The seeds remembered their green names and became trees.

But Vela’s fire was nearly gone. She dropped into the new grass, dim as ash. The earth hid her gently among the roots.

That is why beetles gleam after rain: they carry sparks of Vela, who opened the sky with her brave little flame.
